h.strategy: After listing and negating default assumptions, keep only the negations that a general mechanism supports. Candidate mechanisms: parent quality (strong parents leave little room to improve and have more to lose), redundancy (duplicate or similar options dilute each other's contribution), and bottlenecks (an option matters little when it is not on the path to the output, however strong it is). Prefer predictions in which a usually helpful edit becomes neutral or harmful in a common context, or a usually harmful edit becomes harmless. Avoid conditions that only a few parents satisfy. Spread hypotheses across different edited fields and condition fields. Give at least four 'lower' predictions where the intuitive guess would be 'higher'.

hyps.why: With edge 4 cut, node 1 reaches the output only via edge 2 then edge 5, so a stronger edge 0 is a partial bottleneck and gains less.
Replacing a strong conv on the direct edge with a skip loses capacity, unlike replacing weaker ops.
With edge 1 cut, node 2 is fed only through edge 2, so upgrading edge 5 has less signal to refine.
A strong conv on the parallel direct path makes another conv path redundant, leaving little headroom.
Edge 5 is node 2's only exit, so with it cut anything computed through edge 2 never reaches the output.
A second skip into the output duplicates the existing shortcut and replaces a useful conv path with no new benefit.
With a skip shortcut already present, an extra conv on a side path adds little and can add optimisation noise.
The direct skip carries the signal, so deleting the inner edge 1->2 is nearly harmless, whereas it usually costs accuracy.
Node 2 cannot reach the output when edge 5 is none, so a stronger edge 1 is useless.
With edge 5 already cut, removing the direct edge leaves only the 0->1->3 path, so the loss is larger than when more paths exist.
